record.title: A preprint tests a lightweight trust gate for conflicting memories in language-model agents
record.summary: An arXiv v1 preprint proposes the Memory Decision Layer, a zero-trained-parameter controller that evaluates retrieved memories before generation using relevance, reliability and task risk, then chooses whether to adopt or abstain. In benchmark experiments with constructed memory conflicts, the authors report lower hallucination rates than standard retrieval-augmented generation in tested settings, including zero hallucinations in the tested high-risk samples for several models. On one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both had 4.8% overall hallucination, while high-risk rates were 0.0% and 11.9%, respectively. The paper reports about 0.14 ms added latency when embeddings are precomputed, but also residual active-action errors. These are single-team paper results, not independent confirmation or evidence of production performance.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v1 paper specifies a zero-trained-parameter Memory Decision Layer between retrieval and generation. It combines relevance, reliability and task-risk signals using orthogonal projections, separates a confidence norm from directional consistency, and maps them to adopt, suppress, silent or opt-out actions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ benchmark setup with constructed conflicting memories, they report that MDL reduced hallucinations relative to standard RAG and yielded 0.0% hallucination on tested high-risk samples across several model settings. On the Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL reported 0.0% high-risk hallucination versus 11.9% for RAG, while overall hallucination was 4.8% for both.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports about 0.14 ms total added latency for its controller and lexical signal aggregation, measured with embeddings precomputed; it also reports residual hallucinations under active memory use and a 55.6% decision accuracy in a high-risk, high-relevance medical subset.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish reliable performance on naturally occurring memory conflicts or production agent workloads. Its reported zero rates apply only to the tested samples; independent replication and broader adversarial evaluation remain open.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported effect has not been independently reproduced; the experimental memory stores were constructed from benchmark correct/incorrect answers and distractors.
Generalization to naturally occurring, multi-turn memory conflicts and production distributions is unknown; tested high-risk zero rates are sample-bounded and an active-action residual error remains.
The latency report treats embeddings as precomputed and does not establish end-to-end production overhead under variable memory-store sizes and concurrent load.

brief.importance_rationale: If a lightweight, interpretable decision stage can reduce harmful adoption of conflicting retrieved memories, it could improve agent reliability in settings where relevance alone is an unsafe trust signal. The reported evidence comes from one preprint using benchmark-constructed memory conflicts and limited model/sample regimes; real deployment effectiveness is not established.
limitations: Single author-team arXiv v1 preprint; no independent replication inspected.
Memory conflicts are constructed from benchmark reference answers and incorrect answers; hallucination scoring uses embedding similarity.
Some model/sample settings are small; reported zero hallucination rates are bounded to tested samples.
The paper reports 8.0% residual hallucination under active decisions and reduced decision accuracy in a high-risk, high-relevance medical subset.
Reported controller latency assumes precomputed embeddings and is not an end-to-end production measurement.
brief.summary: An arXiv v1 preprint proposes the Memory Decision Layer, a zero-trained-parameter controller that evaluates retrieved memories before generation using relevance, reliability and task risk, then chooses whether to adopt or abstain. In benchmark experiments with constructed memory conflicts, the authors report lower hallucination rates than standard retrieval-augmented generation in tested settings, including zero hallucinations in the tested high-risk samples for several models. On one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both had 4.8% overall hallucination, while high-risk rates were 0.0% and 11.9%, respectively. The paper reports about 0.14 ms added latency when embeddings are precomputed, but also residual active-action errors. technical.claimed_result: In one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both report 4.8% overall hallucination; their high-risk rates are 0.0% and 11.9%. The authors report zero high-risk hallucinations on tested samples for several other model settings and about 0.14 ms added latency with precomputed embeddings.
technical.compute_or_cost: Controller plus lexical aggregation is reported at about 0.14 ms per decision with embeddings precomputed. End-to-end costs and production throughput are not established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies the controller, signal calculations, benchmark setup, baselines and measurements. Outcomes and latency remain author-reported and have not been independently verified in this review.
technical.mechanism: A retrieval-to-generation controller combines relevance, reliability and task-risk signals through orthogonal subspaces and meta-memory fusion. It separately exposes confidence magnitude and directional consistency, applies risk inversion, and selects an action including explicit abstention.
technical.regime: TruthfulQA and HaluEval with benchmark-constructed conflicting memories, reference-based hallucination scoring and tested Gemma, DeepSeek and Gemini model backends; some settings have few questions or seeds.
technical.reproducibility: The paper states that public benchmarks and code/configuration are released under MIT; this review inspected the paper but did not run code or reproduce results.
technical.strongest_baseline: Standard RAG with the same question, model, sampling and constructed memory store; additional comparisons include memory-free generation, CRAG and Self-RAG variants and supervised classifiers.

brief.title: A preprint tests a lightweight trust gate for conflicting memories in language-model agents
brief.why_it_matters: A decision stage between retrieval and generation could let agents abstain when retrieved memories conflict or carry high task risk, addressing a failure mode that relevance scoring alone does not handle. The paper reports benchmark improvements with low controller latency, but the memory conflicts are constructed, the sample regimes are limited, and real-world effectiveness remains unestablished.
